author: claude
title: Understanding the Readback and Hearback Process

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When you listen to air traffic control, pilots seem to repeat almost everything the controller says. Why is that?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's called a readback. When a controller gives an instruction, especially an air traffic clearance, the pilot repeats the key parts back. For example, the altitude, the heading or the runway.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Isn't it a waste of time on a busy frequency?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It takes a few seconds, but it prevents serious mistakes. Radio messages can be unclear. A pilot might hear 'two thousand' when the controller said 'ten thousand.' The readback makes those mistakes visible.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And then the controller has to check it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. That's the hearback. The controller listens carefully to the readback and confirms it's correct. If something is wrong, the controller corrects it right away.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So it's a two-way safety check.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. But it only works if both sides really pay attention. One known problem is expectation. If a controller expects a correct readback, they might not notice a small error.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Similar call signs are a big one. If two flights have names like 'four five six' and 'four six five,' a pilot might accept an instruction meant for the other plane. That's why pilots always include their call sign in the readback. It shows exactly who is answering.
